intuition: First use a slow and a fast pointer to find a meeting inside a cycle. The meeting is not necessarily the entrance. Start a new pointer at the head, then move it and the meeting pointer one link at a time. Their next meeting is the entrance.

Inside a cycle, a pointer moving two links per round gains one position per round on a pointer moving one link. They eventually meet. That meeting need not be the entrance; it only establishes a distance relationship between the path before the cycle and the cycle itself.

At the meeting, fast has traveled twice as far as slow, so their traveled-distance difference is a multiple of the cycle length. Reset one pointer to head and move both one link per round. Their offsets now align exactly at the entrance. If fast reaches None first, the list is acyclic.

steps: For nodes [3,2,0,-4] with pos=1, the tail links back to the original node carrying value 2.
After the first round, slow is at 2 and fast is at 0.
After the second round, slow is at 0 and fast is at 2. After the third, both are at -4.
The meeting at -4 detects a cycle, but -4 is not its entrance. Reset entrance to the head node 3.
Move entrance and slow once: entrance reaches 2, and slow follows the tail’s back-link to that same node 2.
Return that original node. The adapter reports its zero-based index, 1, rather than identifying it only by its value.

codeNotes.note: Taking two links is safe only if both fast and its next node exist; reaching an endpoint also proves there is no cycle.
Identity detects the same node. Value equality could incorrectly report a meeting between distinct equal-valued nodes.
Equal-speed motion after resetting one pointer uses the meeting-distance relation to find the entrance, rather than returning the initial meeting.

keyDecision: If the fast pointer reaches the end, return no entrance. Otherwise use the second, equal-speed phase.

concept.question: Why is the first meeting inside a loop different from its entrance?
intuition: A slow-fast meeting proves a cycle but may happen anywhere inside it. Returning that meeting directly can identify the wrong node.
After detecting a meeting, place one bookmark back at the start. Move it and the meeting bookmark one link per round. The loop-distance relationship makes their next meeting occur at the entrance.
concept.observation: The detection meeting is not the answer; equal-speed walkers locate the entrance afterward.
approach: Detect a meeting with one-link and two-link walkers.
Restart one bookmark at the original head.
Move both one link until their node identities match.
concept.correctness: At detection, the fast walker has traveled twice the slow distance, so the extra traveled distance is a whole number of loop lengths. This makes the distance from the meeting to the entrance, modulo the loop length, equal to the head-to-entrance distance. Equal-speed walkers from those two starting points therefore first meet at the entrance.

complexity.explanation: Detection and entrance location each require only linear link traversal. A few node bookmarks use constant extra memory.

pitfalls: Do not return the initial detection meeting.
Keep node identity in both phases.

scenes.title: Detection meets at minus four
scenes.narration: In 3 → 2 → 0 → -4 → 2, slow and fast first meet at -4 after three rounds.
scenes.decision: The entrance is 2, so the detection meeting is not yet the answer.

scenes.title: Restart a bookmark at the head
scenes.narration: Place one bookmark at 3 and leave the other at -4. Both now move one link per round.
scenes.decision: The cycle-distance relation aligns their remaining distances to the entrance.

scenes.title: They meet at the entrance
scenes.narration: One move sends both to the original node 2. Return that node; the fixture reports its original position 1.
scenes.decision: The answer is an existing node, not a new node with equal value.
